title: Shoemaker v. United States
lead: A federal park commission condemns Rock Creek land after most owners reject voluntary sales. The owners challenge the commission’s composition, the acquisition process and the valuations, including disputed mineral ownership.

actors.name: Pierce Shoemaker’s heirs, devisees and executors
actors.role: Successors and representatives pursuing objections after Shoemaker died during the proceedings.

actors.name: Rock Creek Park commission
actors.role: Three specially appointed civilians plus the Army Chief of Engineers and the District’s Engineer Commissioner.

actors.name: United States
actors.role: Acquiring sovereign and holder of the final condemned title.

actors.name: The President
actors.role: Approved negotiated or appraised purchase prices for government acquisition.

proceedings: The District court rejected an initial constitutional objection; attempted immediate review failed as interlocutory.
Appraisers reported in December 1891; the court confirmed values, ordered deposits in May 1892 and entered final condemnation July 16, 1892.
The Supreme Court affirmed on January 16, 1893, reviewing preserved objections through writ of error from the final decree.
limits: This source-brief narrative states the historical District of Columbia taking without a new opinion audit or current-law certification. The Supreme Court did not define federal condemnation powers within states or decide claims of actual benefit-assessment payers. Adopted lower-court mineral opinions are not separate Supreme Court writings. The resident report lacked its closing page, supplied in the source brief from the judicial reproduction.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Congress authorizes a park and assigns work to existing officers
sections.cue: How did the acquisition and appraisal system work?
paragraphs: Congress’s September 27, 1890 law authorized Rock Creek Park in the District of Columbia for public enjoyment, limited to 2,000 acres. It appropriated $1,200,000 for acquisition and related expenses, half charged to District revenues. A five-member commission would select and survey land: three civilians appointed by the President with Senate consent, plus the already presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed Army Chief of Engineers and District Engineer Commissioner. A majority could act.

The commission first sought voluntary purchases at presidentially approved prices. If agreement failed, the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia appointed three competent, disinterested appraisers. The President then decided whether those prices were reasonable for acquisition. Payment, or judicial deposit if an owner refused payment, completed transfer. Separate provisions permitted assessments on specially benefited nearby property, with notice and review. Selecting land, appraising compensation and assessing benefits were distinct functions.

sections.title: Most selected owners do not agree to sell
sections.cue: What happened between the initial map and the final transfer?
paragraphs: The initial map was recorded April 16, 1891. Only five of eighty-four selected tracts were acquired by agreement, so the commission petitioned the District court May 20. Pierce Shoemaker died afterward; heirs and devisees were substituted, and his executors challenged the process. Objections concerned appointments, the President’s role, the appropriation cap, park public use, valuation, claimed gold deposits and later omission of mapped tracts.

The court rejected the initial constitutional attack. Immediate review attempts failed because the ruling was interlocutory. Appraisers heard evidence and reported in December 1891; the court overruled exceptions and confirmed values. To fit the appropriation, the commission reduced the acquisition area, and the President approved appraised prices for that selection in April 1892.

Owners declined the awards and demanded interest from the first map. In May the court ordered deposits without that interest. Its July 16, 1892 final decree vested fee-simple title in the United States and directed possession. The owners then obtained a writ of error bringing both the final taking and preserved earlier objections before the U.S. Supreme Court.

sources.pinpoint: Preserved objections and final condemnation; 147 U.S. 287–296

sections.title: The Court treats the engineers’ park work as germane additional duties
paragraphs: Justice Shiras wrote for the Court. The owners argued that because the three civilians were officers requiring nomination and confirmation, the two engineer commissioners likewise required new appointments; Congress could create but not fill offices. The Court accepted the constitutional concern but rejected that characterization.

Both engineers already held constitutionally appointed offices. Congress could enlarge those offices with germane responsibilities without repeating nomination, confirmation and appointment. These park functions were not dissimilar to or outside the sphere of the officers’ existing duties, even though the military/civil line might sometimes be difficult. This was added work for existing officers, not congressional selection of new officeholders for unrelated posts.

The District court had alternatively reasoned that the three civilians could act as a valid majority even if the other memberships were irregular. The Supreme Court instead upheld the germane assignments themselves. It did not authorize assigning any preferred person an unrelated new office.

sources.pinpoint: Why Congress did not make a new appointment; 147 U.S. 289, 300–301

sections.title: Public use and the acquisition safeguards defeat further constitutional objections
sections.cue: What did the President and spending ceiling actually control?
paragraphs: A park for recreation, health or business served a public use. Courts could test that classification; the land quantity then fell to legislative discretion subject to compensation. Congress’s exclusive District legislation combined national and municipal authority. The decision did not define federal taking powers within a state.

Maryland’s cession proviso preserving private property prevented treating cession itself as a transfer of all private land. Read with the grant of full jurisdiction, it did not surrender the power of later compensated public acquisition.

Presidential approval did not adjudicate an owner’s entitlement. Agreement or appraisal fixed price; the President decided whether the government would acquire on those terms. He could decline, not take while ignoring the appraised amount. Likewise, the appropriation capped total expenditure rather than depressing individual valuation. Reducing the acquisition when the full map exceeded funds was permissible; the initial map facilitated negotiation without irrevocably committing every tract.

The Court recognized power to charge proportionate costs to specially benefited property, but declined extended review because no specific error was assigned, no special request had been made below and no appellant was shown actually assessed. It did not decide all possible payer objections.

sections.title: Appraisal review does not become a new judicial valuation trial
sections.cue: How were speculative value and the asserted gold deposits treated?
paragraphs: Appraisers could use inspection and informed judgment alongside submitted evidence. Their oath required faithful, just and impartial valuation by their best skill and judgment, not disregard of evidence. The Court approved present cash-market-value instructions excluding speculative enhancement from the park project. Disagreement among witnesses or dissatisfaction with the amount did not transfer the appraisers’ function to judges; gross error indicating prejudice, corruption or plain mistake remained reviewable.

For alleged gold in tract 39, the Court adopted Justice Cox’s lower-court title analysis that any deposits belonged to the United States. Proprietary patents expressly reserved royal mines; Maryland’s Revolutionary confiscation and cession then carried public property to the United States. This specific chain differed from the ordinary rule that land ownership includes unreserved minerals.

A 1760 patent without a reservation did not supersede the accepted, inconsistent 1772 resurvey grant containing one. Acceptance surrendered the earlier title between grantor and grantee, though older papers could matter to third-party priorities. A later deed of a confiscated cotenant’s interest transferred that interest, not separately reserved mines. Maryland could not convey former public property after its 1791 cession; an 1800 warrant and 1803 patent supplied no alternative mineral title. Preservation of private-right law and judgments did not preserve Maryland’s power over ceded public land. The adopted analysis covered both the original ruling and additional evidence offered on an unsuccessful rescission motion.

sources.pinpoint: Valuation, mineral ownership; 147 U.S. 303–320 & adopted-opinion note

sections.title: The timing of possession defeats the requested interest
sections.cue: What did the final affirmance establish?
paragraphs: The Court rejected interest from filing the map to judicial deposit. Filing had not deprived the owners of possession; they continued receiving rents, issues and profits while compensation was fixed. Delay inconvenience was presumed reflected in the award. There was no interest agreement or failure to pay an already due assessment, and deposit equaled payment when owners declined it. That explanation addressed these timing facts, not a universal rule against interest in condemnation.

On January 16, 1893, the Supreme Court affirmed the District court’s judgment. The taking, title transfer and possession order stood. The report has one Supreme Court opinion, no separate concurrence or dissent and no individual vote tally. The lengthy adopted mineral-title decisions remain lower-court reasoning expressly accepted by the Court, not additional Supreme Court opinions.

The assigned appointments passage isolates germane duties; the complete source brief also preserves the condemnation and valuation decisions. Its source record supplies the final judicial passage and affirmance from the archived reproduction because the resident report scan stops before page 322.
